text: Lesson 20 gave you real classical baselines. This lesson is about the discipline of comparing a quantum method against them fairly -- because it is remarkably easy, even without any intent to mislead, to construct a comparison that looks like a quantum win but isn't one.

Benchmarks go wrong in four common ways. First, comparing against a weak classical baseline -- Lesson 20 showed plain greedy fails 25% of the time on a trivial graph, so beating it alone proves little. Second, reporting query count without query cost -- a '1,000x fewer queries' headline means little if each quantum query is far slower or noisier than a classical sample. Third, cherry-picking problem size or instance -- a method might shine on a small, specially structured case while losing badly at realistic scale.

The fourth way benchmarks go wrong is excluding classical overhead that's actually part of the pipeline -- building the QUBO, converting to Ising form, running the classical parameter optimizer across potentially hundreds of circuit evaluations. A fair comparison times the entire pipeline, end to end, on both sides. And it needs the quantum and classical methods solving the literal same problem instance, judged by the same explicit, shared success criterion, applied identically to every method being compared.

Before trusting any quantum-versus-classical benchmark, run this checklist. Is the classical baseline the strongest reasonably available, not a weak one? Is the comparison metric clearly specified and applied identically to both sides? Is the tested problem size representative, or cherry-picked? And does the timing account for the full pipeline, including classical pre- and post-processing, on both sides? A benchmark that answers all four transparently is rare, genuinely useful, and worth taking seriously.

Next lesson applies this exact standard directly to the published literature, answering plainly where QAOA and VQE currently stand against the best classical alternatives -- separating what's proven from what's promising from what's marketing.
